name: Autosomal recessive hypophosphataemic rickets
specialty: Metabolic bone medicine / Clinical genetics / Nephrology

clinicalPearls: A rare FGF23-mediated phosphate-wasting rickets inherited recessively; the two principal subtypes are ARHR1 from DMP1 variants and ARHR2 from ENPP1 variants.
Children present with rickets, including bowing of the legs, widened wrists, delayed walking, bone pain, short stature and spontaneous dental abscesses, together with renal phosphate wasting.
The key biochemical signature is a low serum phosphate with inappropriately normal or low active vitamin D, driven by non-suppressed or elevated FGF23.
ENPP1-related disease (ARHR2) is allelic with generalised arterial calcification of infancy, so some patients have a history of infantile arterial calcification before developing rickets.
It is distinguished from the far commoner X-linked hypophosphataemia (PHEX) and from autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets (FGF23) mainly by inheritance pattern and associated features.
Hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria (SLC34A3) is a key mimic but shows appropriately high active vitamin D with hypercalciuria and is FGF23-independent.
Dental abnormalities, including spontaneous abscesses and enamel or dentine defects, are common and reflect the mineralisation defect.
Treatment aims to heal rickets with phosphate and active vitamin D, and increasingly with FGF23-directed therapy, while avoiding nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism.
reference.pathophysiology: Autosomal recessive hypophosphataemic rickets is a group of disorders unified by excess bioactivity of fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23), a bone-derived hormone that reduces renal phosphate reabsorption by down-regulating the sodium-phosphate cotransporters and suppresses activation of vitamin D. In ARHR1, biallelic loss-of-function variants in DMP1 (dentin matrix acidic phosphoprotein 1), an osteocyte matrix protein, disrupt osteocyte regulation of mineralisation and lead to increased FGF23. In ARHR2, biallelic variants in ENPP1 (ectonucleotide pyrophosphatase/phosphodiesterase 1) reduce generation of inorganic pyrophosphate; deficiency of the same enzyme underlies generalised arterial calcification of infancy, and secondary elevation of FGF23 produces phosphate wasting and rickets. The final common pathway of renal phosphate wasting with impaired vitamin D activation causes defective bone and dental mineralisation, giving rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.
additionalDifferentials: X-linked hypophosphataemia (PHEX), the commonest inherited form
Autosomal dominant hypophosphataemic rickets from FGF23 gain-of-function variants
Hereditary hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria (SLC34A3), which is FGF23-independent
Fanconi syndrome with renal phosphate wasting
Nutritional vitamin D-deficiency rickets and vitamin D-dependent rickets
Fibrous dysplasia or McCune-Albright syndrome with FGF23 excess
additionalInvestigations: Serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone
Assessment of renal phosphate handling, including the tubular maximum reabsorption of phosphate relative to glomerular filtration rate
Intact FGF23 measurement, which is inappropriately non-suppressed or elevated
Active and storage vitamin D metabolites
Radiographs of the wrists and knees for rickets, with a skeletal survey as needed
Molecular testing of DMP1 and ENPP1, with PHEX, FGF23 and SLC34A3 for the differential
Renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis, and vascular imaging if ENPP1-related arterial calcification is suspected
redFlags: Features of infantile arterial calcification in ENPP1-related disease, with cardiovascular compromise
Progressive skeletal deformity, fractures or severe bone pain
Nephrocalcinosis or deteriorating renal function during treatment
Dental sepsis arising from spontaneous abscesses
reference.prognosis: With treatment, rickets can heal and growth improve, but deformity, short stature and dental problems may persist; ENPP1-related disease carries added cardiovascular risk from arterial calcification, and lifelong monitoring for treatment complications such as nephrocalcinosis and hyperparathyroidism is required.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing as nutritional rickets and treating with vitamin D alone, which does not correct the phosphate wasting
Missing a history of generalised arterial calcification of infancy in ENPP1-related disease
Confusing it with hypophosphataemic rickets with hypercalciuria, where active vitamin D is already high and adding more risks hypercalciuria
Over-treatment causing nephrocalcinosis and tertiary hyperparathyroidism
Assuming X-linked inheritance and overlooking the recessive pattern or consanguinity
references: Paediatric nephrology and endocrinology reference texts
management: Conventional replacement with oral phosphate salts and an active vitamin D analogue such as calcitriol or alfacalcidol to heal rickets and osteomalacia
Consider burosumab, an anti-FGF23 monoclonal antibody, as targeted therapy for the FGF23-driven phosphate wasting
In ENPP1-related disease (ARHR2) undertake cardiovascular surveillance for arterial calcification, with emerging ENPP1 enzyme-replacement therapy under specialist care
Monitor serum phosphate, calcium, alkaline phosphatase and parathyroid hormone, with renal ultrasound for nephrocalcinosis and vigilance for tertiary hyperparathyroidism
Manage deformity with physiotherapy and orthopaedic review, and provide dental surveillance for spontaneous abscesses
Offer genetic counselling and family screening, noting autosomal recessive inheritance and increased risk with consanguinity
Coordinate through a metabolic bone service with nephrology and, in ARHR2, cardiology input
